lead: Shallow parsing, also called chunking, groups the words of a sentence into short flat units — noun phrases, verb phrases, prepositional phrases — without building a tree inside each unit. It exists because many tasks need only the boundaries of these units, and a chunker is far cheaper and faster than a full parser. A named-entity recogniser, an information-extraction rule, or a parser that has failed on a long sentence can all work from chunks. This chapter shows the IOB tag scheme, how chunking becomes sequence labelling, and how to score it.
prereq: You need: 3.1 for phrase types and Unit 2 for POS tagging and CRF tagging.

blocks.text: A chunk is a short, non-overlapping, non-nesting group of words that acts as one unit. A base noun phrase is the noun phrase without a following prepositional phrase: in “the cake in the park”, the chunk is “the cake”, not the whole phrase. Common chunk types are NP (noun phrase), VP (verb phrase), PP (prepositional phrase), ADJP (adjective phrase) and ADVP (adverb phrase). Each word belongs to at most one chunk, and chunks never sit inside each other. Words that belong to no chunk carry the label O, meaning outside.

A rule-based chunker matches patterns over POS tags. The pattern Det? Adj* N+ means an optional determiner, any number of adjectives, then one or more nouns. It matches “the cake”, “a red car” and “fresh milk”. A chink is a word or pattern that cannot be inside a chunk and therefore breaks it — a verb between two nouns, for example. Some chunkers find chunks and chinks together, then label the chunks.

Shallow parsing is shallow because it stops at the boundary. You learn that “the cake” is an NP, but not how the determiner and noun combine inside it. That missing tree is exactly what 3.3 builds. For phrase types, see 3.1.

Chunking is written as one tag per word using IOB tags, in the IOB2 convention where every chunk starts with B-. B-X begins a chunk of type X; I-X continues a chunk of type X; O is outside every chunk. A B- tag always opens a new chunk of its own type. An I- tag can only follow a B- or I- with the same type. So “B-NP I-NP” is one NP, while “B-NP B-NP” is two NPs.

items: Write the words in order with their POS tags.
Mark the first word of each chunk B-X, where X is that chunk's type (for example B-NP, B-VP, B-PP).
Mark later words of the same chunk I-<type>.
Mark every word outside a chunk O.

blocks.text: BILOU is a five-tag variant: B begin, I inside, L last, O outside, U unit, where U is a one-word chunk. It makes the end of a chunk explicit.

Because each word gets one tag, chunking is sequence labelling: input is the word/POS sequence, output is the IOB sequence. The HMM, MEMM and CRF taggers from Unit 2 apply unchanged — a CRF is common because neighbouring tags constrain each other. The figure shows the tag string for one sentence.

sections.h3: Scoring chunks and where they are used

blocks.text: Score chunks, not tokens. A predicted chunk is correct only when its start, its end and its label all match a gold chunk. With C correct chunks, N_pred predicted chunks and N_gold gold chunks:
P = C / N_pred, R = C / N_gold, F1 = 2PR / (P + R)
blocks.where: P is chunk-level precision; R is chunk-level recall; F1 is their harmonic mean; C counts chunks with exact boundary and label match; N_pred is the number of predicted chunks; N_gold is the number of gold chunks.

blocks.text: A labelled score uses the type; an unlabelled score ignores the type but still demands exact boundaries. In the example below, one wrong label leaves unlabelled F1 at 1.0 while labelled F1 falls to 0.75.

Uses: named-entity recognition often starts from NP chunks and then classifies each chunk (see Unit 2); information extraction writes patterns over chunk sequences; a fast partial parse gives a first analysis of a long stream; and when a full parser fails or is too slow, chunks are the fallback. Chunks also feed semantic-role labelling (see Unit 4). They are not a substitute for a tree when the task needs internal structure or long-distance attachment.

examples.question: A sentence has gold chunks [The boy]NP, [ate]VP, [the cake]NP and [in the park]PP. A chunker outputs [The boy]NP, [ate]VP, [the cake]NP and [in the park]NP. Compute labelled and unlabelled precision, recall and F1 for the chunker.
steps: Count predicted chunks: N_pred = 4. All four predicted spans are among the four gold spans, but the last label is NP instead of PP.
Labelled matches: the first three predicted chunks match a gold chunk in both boundary and label; the last does not. So C_lab = 3.
Labelled precision = 3/4 = 0.75; labelled recall = 3/4 = 0.75; labelled F1 = 2×0.75×0.75/(0.75+0.75) = 0.75.
Unlabelled matches: all four predicted boundaries equal the four gold boundaries, so C_unlab = 4. Unlabelled precision = 4/4 = 1.0; recall = 4/4 = 1.0; F1 = 1.0.
examples.answer: Labelled precision, recall and F1 are all 0.75; unlabelled precision, recall and F1 are all 1.0.
examples.check:
pred = [("The boy", "NP"), ("ate", "VP"), ("the cake", "NP"), ("in the park", "NP")]
gold = [("The boy", "NP"), ("ate", "VP"), ("the cake", "NP"), ("in the park", "PP")]
lab_correct = sum(1 for p in pred if p in gold)
lab_p = lab_correct / len(pred)
lab_r = lab_correct / len(gold)
lab_f = 2 * lab_p * lab_r / (lab_p + lab_r)
pred_bounds = [p[0] for p in pred]
gold_bounds = [g[0] for g in gold]
unlab_correct = sum(1 for b in pred_bounds if b in gold_bounds)
unlab_p = unlab_correct / len(pred)
unlab_r = unlab_correct / len(gold)
unlab_f = 2 * unlab_p * unlab_r / (unlab_p + unlab_r)
print(lab_p)
print(lab_r)
print(lab_f)
print(unlab_p)
print(unlab_r)
print(unlab_f)

traps: Scoring token-level accuracy instead of chunk-level precision and recall; token accuracy stays high even when every boundary is shifted.
Counting a chunk as correct when its boundary is right but its label is wrong. Only the labelled score punishes that; the unlabelled score does not.
Letting an I- tag continue a chunk of a different type. B-NP must open a new NP; I-VP cannot follow B-NP.
Assuming chunks nest or overlap. IOB assigns each word at most one chunk tag, so nested or crossing chunks need a richer scheme.
Calling a chunker a full parser. It gives flat spans and labels, not a tree, so it cannot answer attachment questions.

quiz.q: In IOB tagging, what does B-NP mean?
quiz.a: B-NP begins a noun-phrase chunk: the word starts a new NP and is not a continuation of an earlier chunk.

quiz.q: Why is chunking called shallow parsing?
quiz.a: It gives flat groups with boundaries and labels but no internal tree, so it is one level deep, not a full phrase-structure parse.

quiz.q: Give the IOB tags for “The tall girl sang a song”, using NP, VP and O.
quiz.a: The/DT B-NP, tall/JJ I-NP, girl/NN I-NP, sang/VBD B-VP, a/DT B-NP, song/NN I-NP.

quiz.q: A chunker predicts 5 chunks. The gold standard has 4 chunks. Exactly 3 predicted chunks match a gold chunk in boundary and label. Compute labelled precision, recall and F1.
A system gets every chunk boundary right but labels one NP as PP. Which score drops: labelled or unlabelled? Explain.
quiz.a: The unlabelled score stays at 1.0 because every boundary is exact. The labelled score drops because that chunk's type does not match the gold type, so it is not an exact labelled match.

quiz.q: Name the five BILOU tags and state the job of each.
quiz.a: B begin, I inside, L last, O outside, U unit. U marks a one-word chunk; L marks the final word of a multiword chunk.

quiz.q: Why can an HMM or CRF tagger built for POS tagging be reused for chunking?
quiz.a: Chunking is sequence labelling: one input token gives one output tag, just as in POS tagging. The model learns tag transitions and word/POS emissions, so the same training and decoding code works with IOB tags as the output labels.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, chunkers run as the first stage of resume parsers, invoice readers and search-query analysers, where a full parse would be too slow. Neural taggers now often replace CRFs, but the IOB output format is the same, so evaluation code and downstream rules still work. Research extends chunking to nested and discontinuous chunks, where flat IOB is not enough and span-based models are used. Search for chunking shared tasks, BILOU tagging and span-based chunking to go further.
